processing: A green tea fixed by heat, shaped and dried; made today in several styles, including Jiukeng Maojian and Longjing from the Jiukeng plant.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Zhejiang greens, with the earliest and most tender picks fetching the most.
appearance_dry: Robust, straight, tender-green leaves when made in the Longjing style.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow-green, as is typical of Zhejiang greens.
appearance_wet: Stout, tender green leaf and bud, typical of a robust seed-grown plant.
taste_profile: Clean, high fragrance and a fresh, brisk taste with some body from the sturdy leaf.

brewing.notes: A sturdy green that can take water a little warmer than a delicate pre-Qingming Longjing.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, as usual for Zhejiang greens, and best within a year. The name can mean the place, the plant or a tea made from it, so check whether a Jiukeng Longjing or a Jiukeng Maojian is on offer.
description:
Jiukeng is a name doing three jobs: a township in Chun'an county by Qiandao Lake, the old tea from there, and a well-known seed-propagated tea plant. It is one of China's first nationally recognised seed-grown cultivars, planted well beyond its home.

Because it grows from seed, a Jiukeng garden is a mix of slightly different plants, which is part of its value to breeders. The leaf is made into plain regional greens, into Jiukeng Maojian, and into Longjing with a sturdier look than the slim modern cultivars.

The common description is a robust leaf with a tender green colour, a clear high aroma and a fresh, brisk taste. It has more grip than the softest Longjing, so it suits slightly warmer water and is forgiving for everyday brewing.

Look for the spring date and whether the pack names Chun'an or Qiandao Lake, because the cultivar grows elsewhere. Jiukeng township has also pushed organic production in recent years, so organic labels are common here. Promotional claims that West Lake Longjing descends from Jiukeng and that it is the mother of China's tea plants are worth taking with some salt.
history:
Its documented fame is old. Li Zhao's Tang-dynasty Tang Guoshi Bu lists Muzhou's Jiukeng among the notable teas of its day, and the local gazetteer Yanling Zhi records that Jiukeng tea was tribute under the Tang and that the tribute ended under the Song. A claim of Han-dynasty beginnings is repeated locally but has no firm support.

In modern times the Jiukeng plant was among the first ten seed-propagated cultivars recognised at national level, and Jiukeng Maojian received a geographical indication registration in 2017. Chun'an promotes an old 'tea tree king' in the township, said to be about 800 years old, though that age comes from local publicity.
